description: Snowflake hierarchical queries - [START WITH <pred>] CONNECT BY [PRIOR] c = [PRIOR] c, the LEVEL pseudo-column and CONNECT_BY_ROOT <col>. Every expectation was measured on a live Snowflake account with a two-root fixture, one of them three levels deep. LEVEL is 1 at a root and grows by one per step down; CONNECT_BY_ROOT carries the branch root's value, and without a hierarchy it degenerates to the column's own value. Without START WITH every row seeds its own tree, so the five-row fixture expands to nine hierarchy positions. START WITH may follow CONNECT BY, PRIOR may be written on either side, and the condition may conjoin - but a comma-separated condition list is not Snowflake syntax. WHERE filters the EXPANDED rows and not the walk, so a filtered-out root still contributes its children. A star selects only the SOURCE columns: LEVEL and CONNECT_BY_ROOT are pseudo-columns and never expand from one. Inside a CONNECT BY query LEVEL is the DEPTH even when the table has its own LEVEL column, bare and qualified alike, while outside it the real column keeps its values. A lone START WITH is a syntax error, and GROUP BY / HAVING after a CONNECT BY are rejected. PRIOR and CONNECT_BY_ROOT stay usable as identifiers and as bare table aliases, where ASOF and MATCH_CONDITION do not. Converted 1:1 from query/ConnectByTest (now retired); the Java read individual row indexes, which the converted tests state as whole ordered row sets.

steps.sql: CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT id, nm, LEVEL FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id ORDER BY id
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT LEVEL, CONNECT_BY_ROOT id AS rid, id FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id ORDER BY rid, id
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT CONNECT_BY_ROOT nm AS test_column_alias FROM h ORDER BY 1
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT id, LEVEL FROM h CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id ORDER BY id, LEVEL
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT id FROM h CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id START WITH pid IS NULL ORDER BY id
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT id FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY PRIOR id = pid ORDER BY id
SELECT id FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id AND nm <> PRIOR nm ORDER BY id
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT id FROM h WHERE sal > 15 START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id ORDER BY id
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT * FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id ORDER BY id
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT DISTINCT LEVEL FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id ORDER BY 1
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id
SELECT id FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id ORDER BY id LIMIT 2
SELECT id FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id UNION ALL SELECT 99 ORDER BY id
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT id, LEVEL FROM (SELECT * FROM h) START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id ORDER BY id
WITH c AS (SELECT * FROM h) SELECT id, LEVEL FROM c START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id ORDER BY id
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT id FROM h START WITH id = 999 CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id ORDER BY id
CREATE TABLE lv (level INTEGER, id INTEGER)
INSERT INTO lv VALUES (7, 1)
SELECT level, id FROM lv START WITH id = 1 CONNECT BY id = PRIOR id + 100
SELECT lv.level FROM lv START WITH id = 1 CONNECT BY id = PRIOR id + 100
SELECT level FROM lv
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT id FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL
SELECT LEVEL, COUNT(*) FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id GROUP BY LEVEL
SELECT id FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id HAVING COUNT(*) > 0
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT PRIOR id FROM h

skip.reason: live Snowflake performs no cycle detection - the query simply runs until something cancels it, and on a real account this exact statement runs for hours unless cancelled server-side, the default statement timeout being two days. An in-memory engine cannot hang, so its walk is depth-bounded and reports the cycle: a deliberate divergence, which is why this test must never reach a real account.

steps.sql: CREATE TABLE cyc (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER)
INSERT INTO cyc VALUES (1, 2), (2, 1)
SELECT id FROM cyc START WITH id = 1 CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id
CREATE TABLE kw (prior INTEGER, connect_by_root INTEGER)
INSERT INTO kw VALUES (1, 2)
SELECT prior, connect_by_root FROM kw
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT prior.id FROM h prior ORDER BY prior.id
SELECT * FROM h connect_by_root
SELECT * FROM h asof
SELECT * FROM h match_condition
CREATE TABLE h (id INTEGER, pid INTEGER, nm VARCHAR, sal INTEGER)
SELECT CONNECT_BY_ROOT nm FROM h START WITH pid IS NULL CONNECT BY pid = PRIOR id ORDER BY 1
